entry.title: Markdown to HTML: 0 LLM Tokens for 4 Posts, 23 FAQs Extracted
entry.summary:
We needed to publish four manuscripts (43,699 bytes in total) that another project had handed over, and the obvious move was to ask an LLM to turn the markdown into HTML. We wrote a deterministic converter instead. It used zero LLM tokens, extracted 23 FAQ questions automatically, and all four posts passed its built-in checks. The reason is not cost. The manuscripts already contained values that had been cross-checked by hand, such as notice numbers and page numbers, so changing a single character during formatting would itself be a defect. This post covers the rule we use to decide between a script and an LLM, what the converter actually does, and the two publishing traps it closed without anyone having to remember them.

entry.title: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It
entry.summary: If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place. Image compression operates on pixel data. Metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS coordinates — is stored in structurally separate sections of the file. Whether those sections survive compression is entirely a function of how the tool is built. JPEG files use marker segments to organize data. The pixel stream starts at the SOS (Start of Scan) marker. Metadata lives in application markers: APP1 (0xFFE1) — EXIF and XMP payloads APP13 (0xFFED) — IPTC-IIM data APP2 (0xFFE2) — ICC color profiles Low-level libraries like libjpeg and libjpeg-turbo process only the pixel buffer. entry.title: I’m building Nexy: a Python full-stack framework with compiled .nexy pages and typed frontend actions
entry.summary:
Hi everyone 👋 I’m working on Nexy, an open source Python web/full-stack framework, and I wanted to share it here to get your feedback. I wanted a way to build modern web apps while keeping Python at the center - with a clear developer experience on the frontend, and with performance treated as something you measure, not just promise. Compiled .nexy pages: write Python logic and the view in the same file (compiled by Nexy). File-based or modular routing: pick the structure that fits your project. Typed Python actions for modern frontends: call Python actions from React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or Preact components through a typed interface. SSR and CSR options, integrated with Vite. Measured performance goals: a focus on concrete budgets (startup, reload, request cost), published with their method and machine. Real examples in the repo: a Markdown blog, a Svelte notes app, a Vue store, and a sales-report dashboard. Nexy is still young and evolving, so I’m especially interested in honest feedback. The easiest way to get a feel for Nexy is to browse the docs and try one of the examples: Docs & site: https://nexypy.github.io/nexy/
Repository: https://github.com/NexyPy/nexy
Examples: https://github.com/NexyPy/nexy/tree/develop/examples (see blog, notes, store, sales-report) Feedback on the developer experience and architecture People willing to try an example and tell me what feels good or confusing Contributors interested in the compiler, routing, frontend integrations, docs, or examples If this sounds interesting, I’d really appreciate a try, a ⭐ on the repo, or your thoughts in the comments. GitHub: https://github.com/NexyPy/nexy
Docs: https://nexypy.github.io/nexy/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/nexy-dev/
Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Lightweight API Clients for Low-Memory Machines
entry.summary: Quick answer: On a low-memory machine, the lightest real option is a terminal client such as curl, HTTPie, or xh, followed by a native or Tauri-based desktop GUI. The popular Electron clients bundle a full Chromium runtime per install and usually hold the largest resident set. Treat every memory figure as something you measure yourself, since idle RAM, a large collection, and several open tabs move the number more than the product name does. Two clients can show the same request builder and still cost very different amounts of memory. The difference is usually the runtime underneath. An Electron app ships its own Chromium and Node, then splits work across a main process, a renderer, and a few GPU and utility helpers.
